FINAL, SWITCH = D.FINAL, D.SWITCH

TENTH = num(100 * 10 ** -D.RATE_DECIMALS, 1)  # the inputs' published precision, in points
DWP_TEXT = (D.ROOT / D.DWP["file"]).read_text()

def lower1(t):

def pm(v, e):
    """'£11.4bn ± £0.5bn': a draw average with its 95% Monte Carlo error."""
    return f"{bn(v, 1)} ± {bn(e, 1)}"

PEN = ("pensioners_absolute_ahc", "pensioners_relative_ahc")
pov_c_max = max(abs(pov_change(central, k)) for k in central["poverty_pct"]["triple_lock"][str(FINAL)])

SIM_G = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["G"][FINAL])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}
SIM_Y = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["y"])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}
SIM_BELOW = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["below"])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}
SIM_SW = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["switch"])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}
SIM_SWF = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["switch_floor"])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}
SIM_PREM = {k: D.sim_mean(k, lambda s: s["premium"])[0] for k in ("minus", "plus")}

off_c = sum(MEAN_IN["minus"][y][0] - CSTAT["cpi"][str(y - 1)] for y in FWD) / len(FWD)

WS = D.wedge_split()
ROUND_MAX = max(abs(D.rounding_gap(pid)) for pid in EXCESS)

TRANS = V2["window_years"] - 1
bt_pred, bt_real = A["predicted_switches"]["mean"] / TRANS, A["realised_switches"]["mean"] / TRANS

B1_CLIP = {q: D.b1_sup("c", stat=q) for q in ("p50", "p95")}  # every negative input set to zero

def zero_or(x, f, d=1):
    """A range's end as prose: "zero" when it rounds to zero (a percentile at the paths that save nothing), else f."""
    return "zero" if num(x, d) == num(0, d) else f(x, d)

def range90(lo, hi, f, d=1):
    """The 5th to 95th percentile as prose. When the 5th percentile is zero, more than 5% of paths save nothing and the
    interval from zero holds 95% of paths, not nine in ten, so the 95th percentile is given alone."""
    if num(lo, d) == num(0, d):
        return f"95% of paths save {f(hi, d)} or less"
    return f"nine in ten paths save between {f(lo, d)} and {f(hi, d)}"

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Pension rules paying the highest of several indices ratchet above earnings; we ask what an earnings-anchored rule removes. From April `{python} SWITCH` the UK's adjusted Triple Lock raises the State Pension by the highest of `{python} FLOOR`, CPI and what keeps its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings. Its excess over its earnings path follows a Lindley recursion, so the gap from the triple lock grows only in earnings-led years after price- or floor-led ones. Replayed from April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, it removes `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of the triple lock's excess. A Bayesian model of the uprating inputs, fitted to the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) forecast errors and earlier outturns, puts the median gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` at about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 0)`, with `{python} B1_HALF` of paths above `{python} bn(TEN, 0)`, if forecast errors over `{python} B1_FWD_SPAN` are as large as over `{python} B1_ERR_SPAN`; without `{python} V1_HOT` the median is `{python} bn(B1_S7, 1)`, and with errors the size of past outturn variation `{python} bn(B1_S12, 1)`. About `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[1], 1)` of the median comes from how the statutory inputs differ from calendar-year outturns. On the OBR's central path the saving is `{python} bn(c_g, 1)`.

**Keywords:** `{python} KEYWORDS`. **JEL codes:** `{python} JEL`.

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Indexation rules set how pensions in payment keep pace with prices and earnings, and with them much of a pension system's long-run cost [@vidalmelia2009; @oecd_pag2023]. A rule that pays the highest of several indices each year is asymmetric: it passes on every year in which one index leads and keeps that gain in all later years. We ask which part of such a rule's excess over earnings an earnings-anchored rule removes, on which paths of the indices, and how large the saving is under a forecast of the indices that states its uncertainty.

Since April 2011 the triple lock has raised the State Pension each April by the highest of prices, earnings growth and `{python} FLOOR` (prices measured by the Retail Prices Index (RPI) in its first year and by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) since), except in April `{python} D.HISTORY["suspended_earnings_year"]`, when the law suspended the earnings leg (@sec-background). Because it takes the highest of three figures every year, a year in which prices or the floor run ahead of earnings raises the pension for good, and later rises build on the higher level. The Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) long-term projections assume that the triple lock raises the pension `{python} obr_premium` percentage points a year faster than earnings [@obr_lted2026], and it estimates that by 2029-30 the triple lock will have added `{python} re.search(r"£[\d.]+ billion", D.benchmark("obr_frs_2025")["figure_text"]).group(0)` a year to spending relative to earnings uprating since its introduction [@obr_frs2025].

The UK Government announced the adjusted Triple Lock on 29 September 2026, the day on which the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) published its analysis of the change [@dwp_uprating2026], and Autumn Budget 2026, delivered on 28 October 2026, confirmed it [@budget2026]. The triple lock continues to apply to each uprating up to and including April `{python} SWITCH - 1`; from April `{python} SWITCH`, after a year in which price inflation or the floor exceeds earnings growth, the uprating returns the State Pension towards its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings (@sec-two-rules). The Budget puts the saving at: "`{python} budget_saving`" [@budget2026, para. 1.29], citing DWP's analysis, and it recognises that the saving depends on the path of the indices: "`{python} budget_hard`" [@budget2026, Box 5.A]. We quantify that dependence. The Budget links the saving to funding a new settlement for older people, including personal care in England [@budget2026, chapter 1], and the OBR notes that the long-term effect of the two announcements together depends on that reform's cost [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.54]; we cost the pension change alone.

The adjusted Triple Lock keeps the triple lock's protection against prices and the floor but removes the ratchet: the part of the triple lock's excess over earnings that it keeps after earnings lead again. The adjusted rule still pays above its earnings path while an excess lasts, so its saving is less than the triple lock's whole premium over earnings uprating. We estimate its effect against the triple lock from `{python} fy(D.YEARS[0])` to `{python} fy(FINAL)` with microsimulation runs of PolicyEngine UK [@ahmadi2026] on the whole survey population, on the OBR's central path, with the OBR's long-term triple-lock premium applied to the triple lock only, and on simulated paths of prices and earnings. We forecast its distribution with a Bayesian model of the uprating inputs, and those runs convert its paths to cash.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it gives a closed form for the gap between a max-of-indices rule and its earnings-anchored variant. The anchored rule's excess over its earnings path follows a Lindley recursion [@lindley1952], so the gap grows each year by the smaller of earnings' lead and the excess the anchored rule still carries: it depends on the order of the indices' leads and not only on their average, as a lookback option's payoff does [@goldman1979] (@sec-formal). Two corollaries follow: a costing that enters the triple lock's excess as a smooth premium attributes all of it to the ratchet, and a lead for prices or the floor in the last year saves nothing. Second, it forecasts the saving with its uncertainty, where the official costings give single figures [@dwp_uprating2026; @budget2026]. The forecast comes from a Bayesian vector autoregression in the deviations of the two inputs from a forecast path [@doan1984; @litterman1986], with Student-t shocks, fitted to the OBR's forecast errors since 2011 and to the statutory outturns before them (@sec-b1-method). Third, it tests stochastic models of the uprating inputs against official forecast vintages under a registered pass rule [@casey2012; @olken2015] and reports the negative result: two registered models failed, and a record of `{python} words(n_c4)` yearly forecasts tests any such model only weakly (@sec-test, @sec-discussion). We designed the forecast model after both registered models failed and after we had seen a sensitivity conditional on stated volatility (@sec-v1); no test has passed it, and @sec-b1-method states why we report it.

The main result is the forecast of the saving. If forecast errors over `{python} B1_FWD_SPAN` are as large as over `{python} B1_ERR_SPAN`, the median gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 0)` and `{python} B1_HALF` of paths save more than `{python} bn(TEN, 0)` (@sec-b1). Without `{python} V1_HOT` in the record the median is `{python} bn(B1_S7, 1)`, and with errors the size of past outturn variation `{python} bn(B1_S12, 1)` (@sec-b1). The median exceeds the OBR central path's own saving because the forecast's paths are centred on that path and the saving comes from variation around it. The scenarios check the forecast for robustness (@sec-budget): on the OBR's central and long-term paths the rule removes all of the triple lock's excess over earnings, by construction of a smooth path on which earnings lead in every April after the price- or floor-led ones. The evidence that needs no model of the indices' future is the replay: started in April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, the rule removes `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of the triple lock's excess (@sec-formal, @sec-past).

@sec-background describes the triple lock's record and relates the paper to the literature. @sec-rules states the two rules, derives where the saving comes from and replays the rule on past inputs. @sec-method describes the data, the microsimulation, the paths of prices and earnings, the two registered models that failed their test and the Bayesian forecast model. @sec-results gives the forecast of the saving and what it rests on, then the scenarios as checks of robustness, the mechanism along single paths and the distributional effects. @sec-dwp compares the results with official costings, @sec-discussion discusses what they imply for costing such rules, and @sec-conclusion concludes and states the main limitations. The appendices give the proofs, details of the model and the data, the record of the two registered models and their test, the checks of the Bayesian forecast, diagnostics of the scenarios, the distribution of the saving under stated volatility and four example pensioners.

### Related literature

Automatic adjustment mechanisms link a pay-as-you-go pension system's benefits or contributions to indicators, so that its finances respond to demographic and economic change without new legislation [@vidalmelia2009]; @knell2010 shows how the choice of adjustment factor changes the return such a system pays, @valdesprieto2000 shows which indexation rules keep a notional-account system solvent, and @alonsogarcia2018 design such mechanisms for notional accounts when the economic and demographic inputs are uncertain. The indexation of pensions in payment is one such link. Countries index to prices, to earnings or to a mix of the two, and the choice sets how a pensioner's income moves relative to workers' incomes over a retirement [@whitehouse2009; @barr2009]; the OECD's review of the inflation surge since 2021 records how far different rules protected pensioners' purchasing power [@oecd_pag2023]. In the UK the basic State Pension moved from earnings to price indexation in 1980, one of the reforms whose effects on pensioners' incomes @disney2005 set out. Some rules abroad defer an adjustment and recover it from later rises, as Germany's pension guarantee does through its catch-up factor and Japan's macroeconomic indexation through its carry-over [@oecd_pag2021]; the adjusted Triple Lock is of this kind, with the earnings path as the level to which the pension returns. These studies compare rules by their cost and adequacy on given paths of prices and earnings. We know of none that derives how the cost of a rule paying the highest of several indices depends on the order in which the indices lead. The triple lock takes the highest of three figures each year, and @portes2023 places it in the longer history of the State Pension's value relative to earnings.

A rule that pays the higher of two growth rates and compounds the result has the structure of a path-dependent option. One year's rise is the payoff of an option on the maximum of several assets [@margrabe1978; @stulz1982]. The triple lock's excess over earnings, the sum of each year's lead of prices or the floor over earnings, compounds a yearly local floor, as a cliquet or ratchet guarantee does [@hardy2003; @tiong2000], while the adjusted rule's gap depends on a running minimum of the cumulative difference between the indices, as a lookback option's payoff depends on the running minimum of a price [@goldman1979; @conze1991]. The adjusted rule's excess over its earnings path is a draw-up of that cumulative difference, whose distribution the literature on the maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion describes in continuous time [@magdonismail2004], and Spitzer's identity gives its expectation when the yearly differences are independent [@spitzer1956]. That literature prices such payoffs under a given process for the underlying; we use its identities to state which part of an indexation rule's excess an earnings anchor removes.

The option analogy connects the paper to the valuation of guarantees. @merton1977 values a loan guarantee as a put option, @lucas2012 argues that public guarantees and policies should be valued at market prices that charge for the risk they carry, and @geanakoplos2010 apply that approach to accrued Social Security benefits. In pension finance, @dejong2008 values the liabilities of a fund that indexes benefits only when its funding allows, an option embedded in the indexation rule, and @hoevenaars2008 value the transfers between generations that such contingent rules create. We measure the cost in cash, undiscounted and with no charge for risk, because official costings of uprating rules use that measure and we compare our results with them; a market value of the triple lock's guarantee would also need a price for UK earnings and inflation risk, which we leave aside. We use the option analogy for the structure of the payoff only.

The same guarantee also shares risk between generations. @diamond1977 sets out the framework for analysing social security, and @ballmankiw2007 and @gollier2008 show how a pension system can share risk between generations that cannot trade with each other. Indexation decides who bears the risk in a pay-as-you-go system's returns: @shiller1999 argues for designing social security to share income risk across generations, @bohn2009 shows how fiscal policy and benefit rules allocate aggregate risk between cohorts, and @auerbach2011 compare how sustainable unfunded systems with different adjustment rules spread demographic and economic shocks. The triple lock insures pensioners against years in which prices or the floor beat earnings, permanently and at the expense of later taxpayers; the adjusted rule keeps that insurance only until earnings catch up, and so moves the risk of a fall in the pension relative to earnings back to pensioners for a time. We measure the fiscal side of that transfer, not its welfare value.

Long-run projections of pension spending are uncertain, and stochastic projections of social security finances express that uncertainty as distributions over paths of demographic and economic inputs [@lee1998]. The OBR's fiscal risks and sustainability reports treat the triple lock as a source of fiscal risk and project its cost against earnings uprating [@obr_frs2025]; in the long-term scenarios of its 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, as summarised in the October 2026 outlook, the triple lock accounted for around a third of the projected rise in State Pension spending as a share of GDP [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.48].

Central banks and fiscal analysts publish fan charts to show the uncertainty around a central projection [@britton1998; @celasun2006]. Researchers can test a model that supplies such a distribution against outcomes: probability integral transforms check its calibration [@diebold1998], a forecast should be as sharp as its calibration allows [@gneiting2007calibration; @mitchell2011], and proper scoring rules reward a forecaster for reporting its true predictive distribution [@gneiting2007], including for multivariate outcomes [@scheuerer2015]. Density forecasts of inflation and output are better calibrated when they allow volatility to change over time [@clark2011]; our simulated scenarios do not, and our Bayesian forecast allows it only through fat-tailed shocks. Bayesian vector autoregressions, which shrink the coefficients of a small system towards a prior, are a standard tool of macroeconomic forecasting [@doan1984; @litterman1986; @banbura2010; @karlsson2013]; the tightness of the prior is a choice that the data can inform [@giannone2015]; fat-tailed shocks, which a Student-t distribution supplies [@geweke1993], improve such models' density forecasts [@chiu2017], and the observations after March 2020 call for an explicit treatment of jumps in volatility [@lenza2022]. Actuarial models simulate UK prices and wages jointly over long horizons [@wilkie1995]. Forecasters also size the uncertainty around a projection from their own past errors [@reifschneider2019; @knuppel2014], whose variance changes over time and with the horizon [@clark2020]. Our forecast joins the two: a Bayesian autoregression fitted to the errors of official forecasts, with priors set by judgment.

Official fiscal forecasts have their own evaluation literature, which scores their errors and biases after the event [@leal2008] and finds official growth and budget forecasts optimistic on average, more so at longer horizons [@frankel2011]; we know of no earlier test of a stochastic model of uprating inputs against official forecast vintages before a costing uses its paths.

Static tax-benefit microsimulation applies the rules of the tax and benefit system to a representative survey of households, with behaviour held fixed, and is the standard tool for the distributional analysis of benefit reforms [@sutherland2013]; UKMOD is one such model for the four nations of the UK [@richiardi2021]. Such models can add behavioural responses to the static calculation, as PolicyEngine UK does for labour supply and for capital gains realisations [@policyengine_uk]. Dynamic microsimulation models instead project individual life courses, including pension entitlements, forward in time [@li2013]; DWP's costing of the adjusted Triple Lock uses one (@sec-dwp). The net saving depends on how many newly entitled pensioners claim Pension Credit, and take-up of means-tested benefits responds to the size of the entitlement and the cost of claiming [@pudney2006]; our runs hold each benefit unit's claim decision fixed. Pre-analysis plans fix a study's hypotheses and tests before the researcher sees the data, so that the researcher cannot choose results after the fact [@casey2012; @olken2015], and @christensen2018 review their spread in economics. They are rare in model-based policy costing, where the analyst chooses both the model and its evaluation; @sec-test describes the plan we registered and how it changed after the first scores.

## Policy rules {#sec-rules}

### The two rules {#sec-two-rules}

Under the triple lock the full basic and new State Pension rise each April by the highest of three figures: the CPI 12-month rate for the previous September [@ons_d7g7]; growth in average weekly earnings, whole-economy total pay, in May to July of the previous year [@ons_kac3]; and `{python} FLOOR`. ONS publishes both inputs to `{python} TENTH` point, and both rules here use them at that precision. We index each input by the April it sets: $c_t$ is the September CPI rate and $e_t$ the May–July earnings growth published before April $t$, and $f$ is the `{python} FLOOR` floor. Fiscal year $t$ pays the level set in April $t$.

The adjusted Triple Lock follows the triple lock to April `{python} SWITCH - 1`. From April `{python} SWITCH` let $L_t$ be the pension's level and $A_t$ an earnings path that starts at the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level and grows with May–July earnings, $A_t = A_{t-1}(1 + e_t)$. Then

$$L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + \max(c_t, f)),\; A_t\bigr).$$

The pension never rises by less than the higher of CPI and the floor, and never falls below its earnings path. In April `{python} SWITCH` this rise equals the triple lock's, since the earnings path starts at the same level, so the two rules can first differ in April `{python} SWITCH + 1` and the saving in `{python} fy(SWITCH)` is zero on every path. As a modelling assumption we round any top-up to the earnings path up to the next `{python} TENTH` points, so the pension never ends below that path; a top-up therefore leaves the pension at most `{python} TENTH`% above its earnings path, and the margin does not accumulate, because the rule sets each top-up afresh against $A_t$.

The Budget states the rule: from April `{python} SWITCH` the State Pension rises "`{python} budget_rule`" [@budget2026, para. 5.23 and Box 5.A], and adds that "`{python} budget_ratchet`" [@budget2026, chapter 1]. Its wording fixes the anchor: the pension's value relative to earnings "as reached in April `{python} SWITCH - 1`". DWP says the same in other words: "`{python} dwp_over_time`" [@dwp_uprating2026]. Two choices remain ours. The rule uses the triple lock's measures, September CPI and May–July earnings, and we round the top-up up, as above. The OBR writes that its estimates of the change "depend critically on the order, level and covariation of wage growth and inflation over time" [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.53].

The rule would need primary legislation, because section 150A of the Social Security Administration Act 1992 requires the basic and new State Pension, and the Pension Credit standard minimum guarantee, to rise at least in line with earnings [@ssaa1992_s150a], with a corresponding order in Northern Ireland under section 132A of the Social Security Administration (Northern Ireland) Act 1992 [@ssaani1992_s132a]. In a year when the adjusted Triple Lock returns towards its earnings path, it rises by less than earnings growth; @tbl-path-features counts the Aprils in which it does so on each path run through the microsimulation. The suspension of the earnings leg for April 2022 also needed an Act [@ssuba2021].

Some terms recur. The uprating inputs, or statutory inputs, are September CPI and May–July earnings growth, and the determination year is the year whose inputs set the following April's rise. The switch is April `{python} SWITCH`. An input leads in an April in which it exceeds the others, and a change of lead is a change, between consecutive Aprils, in whether earnings or the higher of CPI and the floor leads. A floor year is a year in which May–July earnings growth is below `{python} FLOOR`. We give differences between levels in log points, hundredths of the difference in natural logarithms, which are close to percentages when small. The analysis plan is the public file in which we registered each test and model before its results (github.com/PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock, file docs/METHOD.md).

### Where the saving comes from

```{python}
ex2 = D.stylised_example()
(c1, e1), (c2, e2) = D.STYLISED
x1 = math.log((1 + max(c1, D.FLOOR)) / (1 + e1))  # the adjusted rule's excess over its earnings path after year one
d2 = math.log(1 + max(c2, D.FLOOR)) - math.log(1 + e2)

def gap_of(ds):
    """G after a run of yearly log differences d_t, from the recursions of the formal statement."""
    x = y = 0.0
    for d in ds:
        y += max(d, 0.0)
        x = max(x + d, 0.0)
    return y - x

# A spread that lowers the gap: around d = (+a, -a), the earnings-led year's difference spread by a either way.
SPREAD_A = 0.02
SPREAD_BASE = gap_of((SPREAD_A, -SPREAD_A))
SPREAD_LOW, SPREAD_HIGH = gap_of((SPREAD_A, 0.0)), gap_of((SPREAD_A, -2 * SPREAD_A))
```

When earnings lead, both rules give the same rise. The rules part only after a year in which the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` beats earnings. Both pay that higher figure, but it lifts the adjusted Triple Lock above its earnings path. When earnings lead again, the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level, while the adjusted Triple Lock rises only by the higher of CPI and the floor until its earnings path catches up. Under the triple lock each such rise stays in the pension's level; under the adjusted rule the level returns to its earnings path over the following years.

A two-year example shows the arithmetic. Suppose CPI is `{python} rate(c1, 0)` and earnings growth `{python} rate(e1, 0)` in the first year, then CPI `{python} rate(c2, 0)` and earnings `{python} rate(e2, 0)`. The triple lock rises by `{python} rate(c1, 0)` and then `{python} rate(e2, 0)`, `{python} rate(ex2["tl"], 2)` in all. The adjusted Triple Lock also rises by `{python} rate(c1, 0)` in the first year, which leaves it `{python} points(x1, 2)` log points above its earnings path, and then by the floor, `{python} FLOOR`, `{python} rate(ex2["plan"], 2)` in all. In the second year earnings lead by `{python} points(-d2, 2)` log points, less than the excess, so the whole lead becomes the gap: the adjusted rule ends `{python} rate(ex2["gap"], 1)` below the triple lock (`{python} points(ex2["points"], 2)` points less cumulative growth). The next subsection states this in general.

### A formal statement {#sec-formal}

Write $m_t = \max(c_t, f)$ for the higher of CPI and the floor that applies in April $t$, and $T_0$ for April `{python} SWITCH - 1`, the last rise under the triple lock alone. With $P_t$ the triple lock's level and $L_t$ and $A_t$ as above,

$$P_t = P_{t-1}\,\bigl(1 + \max(m_t, e_t)\bigr), \qquad L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + m_t),\; A_t\bigr), \qquad A_t = A_{t-1}\,(1 + e_t),$$
with $P_{T_0} = L_{T_0} = A_{T_0}$. Let $d_t = \ln(1 + m_t) - \ln(1 + e_t)$, positive in a year in which CPI or the floor beats earnings, and measure each rule's level against the earnings path, $y_t = \ln(P_t / A_t)$ and $x_t = \ln(L_t / A_t)$. Then

$$y_t = y_{t-1} + \max(d_t, 0), \qquad x_t = \max(x_{t-1} + d_t,\; 0), \qquad y_{T_0} = x_{T_0} = 0.$$
The triple lock accumulates every positive $d_t$, while the adjusted rule's $x_t$ is a cumulative sum reflected at zero, a Lindley recursion [@lindley1952]. With $D_t = \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} d_s$ and $D_{T_0} = 0$, the log gap between the rules, $G_t = y_t - x_t$, is
$$G_t = \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(-d_s, 0) + \min_{T_0 \le s \le t} D_s, \qquad \Delta G_t = G_t - G_{t-1} = \min\bigl(\max(-d_t, 0),\; x_{t-1}\bigr) \ge 0,$$
and
$$0 \le G_t \le \min\Bigl(\sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(d_s, 0),\; \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(-d_s, 0)\Bigr).$$

**Proposition 1.** The gap never falls, and it grows only in a year in which earnings lead while the adjusted rule is still above its earnings path, by the smaller of earnings' lead and the remaining excess. The gap after April $t$ is positive if and only if some year $s \le t$ in which prices or the floor lead ($d_s > 0$) is followed by a later year $r \le t$ in which earnings lead ($d_r < 0$). In particular the gap is zero on any path on which earnings lead in every year and on any path on which they never lead, and a lead for prices or the floor in the final year alone gives no saving. @sec-proof gives the proof.

Because $G_t \ge 0$ on every path, a path on which earnings lead in every year after the switch gives the smallest possible saving, zero. A path close to that, such as the OBR's central path, gives a saving close to zero, and a distribution of paths with changes of lead gives a positive average. Proposition 1 does not say that variation around a given path raises the saving above that path's own. The increment is concave in $d_t$ in a year in which earnings lead, so a spread of that year's difference can lower the gap: on the path $d = (a, -a)$ with $a$ = `{python} points(SPREAD_A, 0)` log points the gap is `{python} points(SPREAD_BASE, 0)` log points, and spreading the second year's difference by $a$ either way, with equal weight, gives gaps of `{python} points(SPREAD_LOW, 0)` and `{python} points(SPREAD_HIGH, 0)`, an average of `{python} points((SPREAD_LOW + SPREAD_HIGH) / 2, 0)`. Under independent normal differences, by contrast, the expected gap does not fall as their variance rises (Proposition 2); the counter-example needs a spread specific to one path. For any model of the inputs the bound above gives $\mathrm{E}[G_t] \le \min\bigl(\mathrm{E}[y_t],\, \mathrm{E}[\sum_s \max(-d_s, 0)]\bigr)$. The increment also says when the saving appears: larger earnings leads use up the excess $x_{t-1}$ faster, so higher earnings growth after a year of high inflation brings the saving forward.

**Proposition 2.** If the yearly differences $d_t$ are independent and identically distributed, then with $S_k = d_{T_0 + 1} + \dots + d_{T_0 + k}$ the expected excess and gap after $n$ rises are
$$\mathrm{E}[y_{T_0 + n}] = n\,\mathrm{E}[d^{+}], \qquad \mathrm{E}[G_{T_0 + n}] = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Bigl(\mathrm{E}[d^{+}] - \tfrac{1}{k}\,\mathrm{E}[(S_k)^{+}]\Bigr).$$
If they are normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, the expected gap is zero at $\sigma = 0$ and does not fall as $\sigma$ rises, for every $\mu$. @sec-proof gives the proof, which rests on Spitzer's identity [@spitzer1956].

Proposition 2 gives a check that needs no simulation, though persistence in $d_t$, such as runs of earnings-led years, and a mean that changes from year to year are outside it. At the mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on the replay's inputs from April `{python} hw_first["first"]` to April `{python} LAST_HIST` (`{python} points(H_MU, 2)` and `{python} points(H_SD, 2)` log points) it gives an expected gap of `{python} points(SP_H[0], 2)` log points over those `{python} words(len(HD))` Aprils and an expected excess of `{python} points(SP_H[1], 2)`, against `{python} points(G_HIST, 2)` and `{python} points(Y_HIST, 2)` on the replay itself (@sec-past). At the pooled mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on each earnings scenario's paths from April `{python} SWITCH` it gives `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][0], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][0], 2)` log points by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, against path averages of `{python} points(SIM_G["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"], 2)` (@tbl-scenarios), and expected excesses of `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][1], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][1], 2)` against `{python} points(SIM_Y["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_Y["plus"], 2)`.

The gross saving in a fiscal year is the difference in basic and new State Pension paid,

$$S^{g}_t = \sum_i w_{it}\,\bigl(b^{\mathrm{TL}}_{it} - b^{\mathrm{A}}_{it}\bigr) \approx \bigl(1 - e^{-G_t}\bigr)\, B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t,$$
where $w_{it}$ is the survey weight of person $i$, $b_{it}$ their basic or new State Pension under each rule and $B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$ total spending on both under the triple lock; the approximation is exact, up to rounding, when each person's amount is a fixed share of the full rate. The net saving is the change in the Government's direct budget balance, $S^{n}_t = \sum_h w_{ht}\,(\tau^{\mathrm{A}}_{ht} - \tau^{\mathrm{TL}}_{ht})$, where $w_{ht}$ is the weight of household $h$ and $\tau_{ht}$ the direct taxes it pays less the benefits it receives, State Pension included. The rounding of the top-up to the earnings path adds a small non-negative term to $x_t$, so the identities, and the proposition's "if and only if", hold for the unrounded rule; in the model runs a rounded top-up can leave a small excess that a later earnings-led year turns into gap. On the paths run through the microsimulation the rounding changes $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` by at most `{python} points(ROUND_MAX, 2)` log points.

### The rule on past inputs {#sec-past}

```{python}
first_group = next(g for g in D.history_groups() if g["changes"])
unchanged = [g for g in D.history_groups() if not g["changes"]]
past_weekly = first_group["model"]["counterfactual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(LAST_HIST)]
actual_weekly = first_group["model"]["actual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(LAST_HIST)]
past_saving = first_group["model"]["saving_bn"][str(LAST_HIST)]
spike = max(rec, key=lambda r: r["cpi"])
replay = D.ENVELOPE["last_decade_replay"]
replay_gap = 100 * (1 - replay["counterfactual"]["level_ratio"][str(LAST_HIST)])
# The OBR's replay statistic is an average over all years of the payment gap; the same average on ours, from the
# earliest start that changes anything to the last April.
avg_years = [y for y in D.HISTORY["years"] if y >= hw_first["first"]]
avg_gap = sum(100 * (1 - first_group["ratio"][str(y)]) for y in avg_years) / len(avg_years)
```

We can check the decomposition on inputs that have already occurred, with no model of their future path. We call figures computed from the uprating inputs alone, with no microsimulation run, rule arithmetic. The replay uses today's revised ONS figures, so that both rules see the same inputs. It differs from the rise paid in April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ_hist])`, by `{python} TENTH` to `{python} num(max(abs(100 * (r["rate"] - r["paid"])) for r in differ_hist), 1)` points, because ONS has since revised the earnings figures, and in April `{python} D.HISTORY_RPI_YEAR`, which RPI set. In April `{python} susp_year` (@sec-background) the replay's earnings path grows by that year's CPI, `{python} rate(susp["cpi"])`, the figure the rise followed, rather than by the published earnings figure. On the replay the triple lock rose `{python} pct(rise["triple_lock"], 1)`, against `{python} pct(rise["earnings"], 1)` for earnings alone and `{python} pct(rise["cpi"], 1)` for prices alone, which leaves it `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above where an earnings link alone would have taken it (`{python} pct(paid_above_earn, 1)` as paid, @fig-history).

@tbl-past and @fig-past replay the adjusted Triple Lock on today's figures from each earlier April. Had it started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, its level in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)` would be `{python} pct(hw_first["gap_pct"], 1)` below the triple lock's on the same inputs. Applied to the full new State Pension actually paid, `{python} gbp(52 * actual_weekly)` a year, that would be `{python} gbp(52 * past_weekly)`. Most of the difference follows April `{python} spike["year"]`, when September CPI of `{python} rate(spike["cpi"])` set a rise `{python} points(spike["cpi"] - spike["earnings"], 1)` points above earnings growth of `{python} rate(spike["earnings"])`; the gap opened in the earnings-led Aprils after it, as the increment formula says. From that start, the triple lock's log excess over its earnings path is $y_t$ = `{python} points(Y_HIST, 2)` log points. That is more than the `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above, which starts in April `{python} first["year"]` and counts April `{python} susp_year` at published earnings, while this earnings path grows by CPI in that April. The adjusted rule removes $G_t$ = `{python} points(G_HIST, 2)` log points of it, or `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)`; the rest is the excess it still carries. Started in `{python} listing([g["label"] for g in unchanged], "or")`, the rule would have paid the same as the triple lock every year, because earnings have led in every April since. In full model runs, State Pension spending in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)` would have been `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"], 1)` lower, and the Government `{python} bn(past_saving["net"], 1)` better off once tax and benefits respond. Averaged over the Aprils from `{python} hw_first["first"]` to `{python} LAST_HIST`, the pension would have been `{python} pct(avg_gap, 1)` below the triple lock.

Starts in the same row give the same levels; changes of lead are counted from the earliest."

## Data and method {#sec-method}

### Model and data {#sec-model}

We compute every saving and household figure for a given path by running PolicyEngine UK [@ahmadi2026; @policyengine_py; @policyengine_uk] on the whole survey population, once under each rule. Like the static models that @sutherland2013 describe, PolicyEngine UK applies the tax and benefit rules of each year to survey households. It can also add behavioural responses; our code switches them off, so behaviour stays fixed in every run (@sec-appendix).

All runs use policyengine `{python} V2["policyengine"]`, which pins policyengine-uk `{python} V2["policyengine_uk"]` and policyengine-core `{python} V2["policyengine_core"]`, with the national Microcosm dataset for `{python} fy(2024)` published with it (`{python} count(V2["households"])` households, whose records are built on the Family Resources Survey) [@microcosm2026]. We use the Enhanced Family Resources Survey, version `{python} V2["efrs"]`, only for the check against DWP's caseloads (@tbl-coverage). A path's CPI and earnings growth replace the model's economic assumptions before the data load, so benefit rates, tax thresholds and earnings follow it, and every run checks that they do. Only the basic and new State Pension differ between the two runs of a path. Under both rules the additional State Pension rises with September CPI and State Pension age follows the law's timetable. We model pension-age Housing Benefit under current law. We give money in cash terms for the UK unless we say otherwise.

The paper's repository (github.com/PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock) holds the code, the analysis plan, every stored result with the random seed of its draws, and the manuscript, whose build script recomputes every number, table and figure from those files without running a simulation. The replay, the Bayesian forecast, the results under stated volatility and the scores of both registered models are rule arithmetic on public ONS and OBR series and on stored outputs of the microsimulation runs, all of which the repository holds, so a reader can reproduce them without survey data. The microsimulation runs need the Microcosm dataset, to which access is controlled [@microcosm2026]; the repository stores their outputs.

```{python}
hist_gc = D.HISTORY["cpi"]["2023"], D.HISTORY["earnings"]["2023"]
```

Three conventions shape the net saving. First, the Pension Credit guarantee rises with May–July earnings under both rules. That is the minimum section 150A requires, and neither the Budget nor DWP's analysis says how the Government will uprate the Pension Credit guarantee under the adjusted Triple Lock, so we take the statutory minimum as the main case; in practice the Pension Credit guarantee has risen by the same percentage as the State Pension in each April since 2022, and by less in earlier Aprils in which prices or the floor set the State Pension's rise (@sec-appendix). If it rose by the same percentage as the State Pension under each rule, it would be lower under the adjusted rule, the Pension Credit offset would be smaller, possibly negative, and the net saving larger (@sec-net gives a lower bound on the effect).

Second, the income tax personal allowance stays at `{python} V2['personal_allowance']` to `{python} fy(V2['pa_frozen_to'])`, as current law sets it, and then rises with each path's September CPI; from April `{python} SWITCH + 1`, when the rules can first differ, the full new State Pension is above it, so a lower pension means less income tax even for a pensioner with no other income. The Budget's Pension Tax Allowance [@budget2026, Table 6.1] lapses after April 2030, before the rules can first differ, and we assume no successor.

Third, Pension Credit take-up follows the dataset's own claim decision for each benefit unit, so a household newly entitled under the adjusted rule claims only if that decision says it would; Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them, and passporting from the guarantee credit follows actual receipt.

### The population in each year {#sec-population}

The dataset represents households in `{python} fy(2024)`, and each record stands for a person of its age in every year. Microcosm calibrates its household weights once, in `{python} V2["anchor_year"]`, and through that year every run uses the dataset's own weights. For later years our code rakes those weights so that the weighted number of people in each of `{python} count(D.RAKE_CELLS)` age and sex cells grows as in the ONS's 2024-based population projection [@ons_npp2024] (@sec-appendix). The rake targets age and sex only and recalibrates no other total, such as incomes, benefit caseloads or the number of households. The dataset does not top-code ages, so we keep every recorded age.

Each person's State Pension type follows from the date of birth that their age implies in each year: those who reach State Pension age before 6 April 2016 are on the basic State Pension, later cohorts on the new one [@pa2014]. A record of a given age therefore moves from the basic to the new State Pension as later cohorts reach that age. We do not simulate deaths, migration or contribution histories, and the dataset leaves out pensioners abroad. Records carried forward from today's pensioners may understate the entitlements of people reaching State Pension age in the 2030s, most of whom will have spent their whole working lives under the new State Pension.

### Paths of prices and earnings {#sec-paths-method}

```{python}
cp = D.CENTRAL["path"]
a27 = cp["april_2027_inputs"]
stat_src = cp["statutory_source"]
q_years = [int(y) + 1 for y, s in stat_src.items() if s == "efo_quarterly"]
cal_src = cp["calendar_source"]
efo_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "efo_calendar"]
sim_switch = D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["switches_per_year"]
MINUS_SHIFT = D.MINUS + SHIFT
```

The OBR central path uses the OBR's October 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook (EFO), published with the Budget, for calendar years to `{python} efo_years[-1]` [@obr_efo2026oct], and the OBR's March 2026 long-term economic determinants after that [@obr_lted2026], which the OBR describes as a projection, not a forecast; the OBR published no long-term determinants with its October forecast. We call the combination the OBR central path. April 2027's State Pension rise uses the published May–July 2026 earnings growth, `{python} rate(a27["earnings"])`, and September 2026 CPI, `{python} rate(a27["cpi"])` [@ons_kac3; @ons_d7g7]. For the Aprils `{python} q_years[0]` to `{python} q_years[-1]` the inputs are the OBR's September-quarter CPI and April–June earnings growth; later Aprils use its calendar-year figures. The OBR forecasts average earnings on a national-accounts measure, which stands in here for May–July average weekly earnings. Both rules share these inputs. A second single path, the OBR long-term path, keeps these inputs and pays the triple lock at the OBR's long-term rate (@sec-budget).

The two earnings scenarios of @sec-budget average the saving over simulated paths. The paths come from a model of monthly changes in the CPI index [@ons_d7bt] and in average weekly earnings [@ons_kab9], fitted to data from 2000 to the latest published month, in which each month's change depends on the previous month's changes in both series and the shocks are past pairs of residuals drawn at random; we call it the baseline model. Every path is then shifted by the same smooth drift so that the average calendar-year growth matches the OBR's forecast in every year, and the earnings scenarios move that drift by `{python} SHIFT` points a year from `{python} FROM`. We run a stratified sample of the model's draws through the microsimulation under both rules. @sec-sim-model gives the model, the scenarios' statutory inputs and the estimator.

```{python}
SR = D.SCREEN_RULE
c1 = D.R["uncertainty_ruling"]["c1_failure"]
c1_hits = re.search(r"coverage (\d+)/(\d+)", c1["common_failure"]).groups()
others_fail = [f for f in forms if f != D.PRIMARY_FORM and not forms[f]["passes"]]
fb_all = [D.C2["scores"]["A"]["suspended"][f]["floor_bias"]["mean"] for f in forms]
fallback = min(passing, key=lambda f: forms[f]["proper_score_ratio_geomean"])
APUB = D.C2["scores"]["A"]["published"][D.PRIMARY_FORM]
fb_se = A[fail_stat]["se_overlap_hac"]
past_pct = D.C2["past_years"][D.PRIMARY_FORM]["suspended"]["realised_percentile"]
gb_all = {f: D.C2["scores"]["A"]["suspended"][f]["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"] for f in forms}
gb_round = sorted({num(v, 2) for v in gb_all.values()})
gb_main = num(A["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"], 2)
gb_others = [f for f in forms if num(gb_all[f], 2) != gb_main]
```

An average over simulated paths needs a model whose paths behave like the real inputs. Before scoring any model we registered a test on past OBR forecasts [@obr_hofd2026], with a pass rule on the coverage of central bands, on biases and on proper scoring rules [@gneiting2007; @scheuerer2015] (@sec-test). The baseline model failed one condition: it expected earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * PRED_FLOOR, 1)` of the years of its `{python} words(n_a)`-forecast test, against `{python} pct(100 * REAL_FLOOR, 1)` in practice, a floor bias above the rule's limit. A second model, built on the OBR's past forecast errors and registered before its scores, met every scored condition but one: its variogram score, a proper score of how the yearly gaps move together, is `{python} num(c4_value, 3)` times the baseline model's, above the limit of `{python} num(c4_limit, 2)` (@sec-c4). The test cannot separate either failing figure from its limit, and it has little power. Under the registered rule the paper therefore reports scenarios, and gives the second model's distribution of the share saved once, in @sec-c4; @sec-b1-method says why the paper nonetheless gives a forecast.

### A Bayesian forecast of the inputs {#sec-b1-method}

```{python}
BF = D.B1_FIT
BP_ = BF["priors"]
BW = BF["convergence"]["worst"]
BRB = BF["radius_bound"]
_b1_pushed = {k: datetime.fromisoformat(v.replace("Z", "+00:00")) for k, v in V2["b1_pushed"].items()}
B1_MIN = {k: round((_b1_pushed[k] - _b1_pushed["spec"]).total_seconds() / 60) for k in ("code", "fit")}
B1_CELLS = BF["data"]["error_cells"]
B1_OT = BF["data"]["outturn_transition_years"]
B1_REC = D.b1_record()
B1_LAST1 = B1_REC["single_cell"][B1_ERR[-1]]  # (origin, horizon) of the last target year's one cell
assert B1_REC["first_origin"] == 2010 and B1_LAST1[1] > 1  # "the June ... Budget forecast"; "years ahead"
B1_SEEDS_CH = D.b1_floor_bias("chronological")
B1_SEEDS_TY = D.b1_floor_bias("target_year")
FB_LIM = D.b1_check("chronological", "A", "|floor_bias|")[1]
B1_GB = [D.b1_check(h, t, "|gap_bias_pp|")[0] for h in ("chronological", "target_year") for t in ("A", "B")]
GB_LIM = D.b1_check("chronological", "A", "|gap_bias_pp|")[1]
B1_SW = D.b1_ppc("switches_per_path")
B1_SDC1 = D.b1_ppc("sd_cpi_h1")
B1_GAP_SHARES = [v["share_at_or_above_realised"] for v in D.B1_GAP_PPC.values()]
assert not D.B1_PPC_OUTSIDE and not any(v["outside_central_98"] for v in D.B1_GAP_PPC.values())
assert B1_SEEDS_CH[3] < B1_SEEDS_CH[2] and B1_SEEDS_TY[3] == 0  # the prose: some chronological seeds miss, every target-year seed
B1_PRIOR_PRED = D.B1_VAL["prior_predictive"]["gross_bn"][str(FINAL)]["p50"]
B1_GATE_WALL = D.B1_GATE["wall_coded"][str(FINAL)]["gross_bn"]["p50"]
B1_HOLD = sum(1 for _ in D.B1_BT["hold_outs"]["chronological"]["fits"])
B1_VG = [c["value"] for h in D.B1_BT["hold_outs"].values() for c in h["checks_against_c2_c4_limits"]
         if c["check"].startswith("variogram")]  # both hold-outs, both tests
B1_FWD_FLOOR = D.B1_VAL["forward_paths_against_history"]  # descriptive: earnings below the floor, forward and 2001-25
B1_CENTRE_E = [D.B1["centre"][str(y)]["earnings"] for y in B1_FWD]  # the centre's earnings growth, 2027-38
B1_POST = BF["posterior"]

def post(k, d=2):
    """A posterior median with its 5th to 95th percentile, as prose."""
    s = B1_POST[k]
    return f"{num(s['p50'], d)} ({num(s['p5'], d)} to {num(s['p95'], d)})"
```

The forecast needs a distribution of the uprating inputs over the next `{python} words(len(B1_FWD))` years. We model how far the two inputs fall from an official forecast path, fit that model to how far they fell from the OBR's past forecasts, and simulate paths around the OBR central path. The model is Bayesian: each parameter has a prior distribution, the data update it to a posterior, and the forecast, the posterior predictive distribution, averages over the posterior, so its spread reflects uncertainty about the parameters as well as future shocks [@karlsson2013].

The model describes how September CPI and May–July earnings growth deviate from a forecast path. With $\varepsilon_t$ the pair of deviations in year $t$, $\varepsilon_t = \Phi\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + u_t$ from $\varepsilon = 0$ at the forecast's origin, where $\Phi$ is a full two-by-two matrix (each input's persistence, and the pass-through from last year's prices to pay and from last year's pay to prices) whose largest eigenvalue in modulus is below `{python} num(BRB["bound"], 2)`, so deviations die out. The shock $u_t$ is bivariate Student-t with $\nu$ degrees of freedom and scale matrix $\Sigma$: a normal shock whose variance a single draw each year scales up or down for both inputs together, so that most years are ordinary and a few, like `{python} V1_HOT`, are several times as volatile for prices and pay at once. It is a Bayesian vector autoregression of order one [@litterman1986] with mean zero at every horizon. Forward, the centre is the OBR central path's statutory inputs (@sec-paths-method), and from determination year 2031, where that path passes from the OBR's forecast to its long-term determinants, each path adds a constant shift to CPI and to real earnings growth that no data here estimate.

Two records inform the parameters, and each year enters once. The first is the OBR's forecast errors, the statutory input less the OBR's calendar-year forecast for the same year: for the June `{python} B1_REC["first_origin"]` Budget forecast and each March forecast to March `{python} B1_REC["last_origin"]`, the cells (pairs of a forecast and a horizon) one to four years ahead that the record holds, `{python} words(B1_CELLS)` cells with target years `{python} B1_ERR_SPAN`; `{python} B1_ERR[-1]` has one cell, the March `{python} B1_LAST1[0]` forecast `{python} words(B1_LAST1[1])` years ahead, because the record holds no figure for `{python} B1_ERR[-1]` from the two forecasts after it. An origin's errors are the process started from zero, so each cell's residual is a draw of $u_t$ with scale $\Sigma_F$. Forecasts made in neighbouring years share target years, so each cell is weighted by one over the number of cells with its target year, and each of the `{python} words(len(B1_ERR))` target years counts once. The second record is the statutory outturns of `{python} B1_OT[0] - 1` to `{python} B1_OT[-1]` around an estimated mean, `{python} words(len(B1_OT))` yearly transitions with scale $\Sigma_O$; earnings before 2001 use national-accounts wages and salaries per employee, as in @sec-v1. The two records share $\Phi$ and $\nu$; $\Sigma_O$'s standard deviations are those of $\Sigma_F$ times factors $\kappa$, and its correlation differs from $\Sigma_F$'s by a shift $\zeta$ on the Fisher scale (the inverse hyperbolic tangent of a correlation, which is unbounded), because variation of outturns around their own mean is not forecast error. The forward paths use $\Sigma_F$. @tbl-b1-priors gives the priors and, for $\Phi$, $\Sigma_F$ and $\nu$, which drive those paths, the posterior.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-b1-priors
#| tbl-cap: "The priors of the Bayesian forecast and, for the parameters that drive the forward paths, their posterior medians with `{python} V1_LO` to `{python} V1_HI` percentiles, in percentage points where they have units. Each prior is a judgment written into the analysis plan before the first fit; we set each after seeing the whole record. A dash marks a parameter whose posterior the paper does not report."
def _n(m, sd):
    return f"Normal, mean {num(m, 2)}, sd {num(sd, 2)}"
def _ln(m, sd):
    return f"Log-normal, median {num(m, 2)}, log-sd {num(sd, 2)}"
ph_m, ph_s = BP_["phi_mu"], BP_["phi_sd"]
body = [
    ["Persistence of each input", _n(ph_m[0], ph_s[0]), "Between no memory and a random walk",
     f"CPI {post('phi_cc')}; earnings {post('phi_ee')}"],
    ["Earnings on last year's CPI", _n(ph_m[2], ph_s[2]), "Pay catching up with past inflation, in part", post("phi_ec")],
    ["CPI on last year's earnings", _n(ph_m[1], ph_s[1]), "Labour costs feeding prices, weaker", post("phi_ce")],
    ["Forecast shock scales, CPI and earnings", _ln(math.exp(BP_["log_sigma_mu"]), BP_["log_sigma_sd"]),
     "Wide around the size of official one-year errors already seen", f"CPI {post('sigma_c')}; earnings {post('sigma_e')}"],
    ["Forecast shock correlation (Fisher scale)", _n(BP_["z_mu"], BP_["z_sd"]), "Common shocks move prices and pay",
     post("rho_F") + " as a correlation"],
    ["Outturn less forecast correlation, Fisher scale", _n(0, BP_["zeta_sd"]), "The two records may differ", "–"],
    ["Outturn to forecast shock scale ratios", _ln(1, BP_["log_kappa_sd"]), "The two records may differ", "–"],
    ["Degrees of freedom of the shocks, less two", f"Gamma, shape {num(BP_['nu_shape'], 0)}, rate {num(BP_['nu_rate'], 1)}",
     "Finite variance, with material mass on fat tails", post("nu", 1) + " degrees of freedom"],
    ["Outturn mean, CPI", _n(BP_["m_mu"][0], BP_["m_sd"][0]), "The inflation target", "–"],
    ["Outturn mean, earnings", _n(BP_["m_mu"][1], BP_["m_sd"][1]), "Target inflation plus real pay growth", "–"],
    ["Long-run shift, CPI, from 2031", _n(0, BP_["delta_sd"][0]), "A small persistent miss of the target", "–"],
    ["Long-run shift, real earnings, from 2031", _n(0, BP_["delta_sd"][1]), "Revisions to productivity growth", "–"],
]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Parameter", "Prior", "Reason", "Posterior median (5th to 95th)"], body, "llll")))
```

The second model's registration said that if it failed the paper would report scenarios only, and that another model would need another registration that counts the failures. After it failed, we decided that the paper should give a forecast that states its uncertainty, on a Bayesian approach. The specification of this section is that registration, written before the model's first fit, but it sets no pass rule: the forecast departs from the registered fallback by our decision, not by a test, so the paper's headline rests on that decision, and both failed verdicts stand. The analysis plan's commit that holds it, with the priors, the checks and how the paper reports them, precedes the model's first code and its first fit in the public record (@tbl-timeline), which shows that order and no more. We set the priors after seeing the whole record of forecast errors, every score of the two failed models and the sensitivity of @sec-v1, so no hold-out below is clean, and the checks are reported whatever they show, not applied as a pass rule.

We sample the posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler [@hoffman2014], a Markov chain Monte Carlo method, in NumPyro, `{python} words(BF["sampler"]["chains"])` chains of `{python} count(BF["sampler"]["warmup"])` warm-up and `{python} count(BF["sampler"]["kept"])` kept iterations. The analysis plan's one hard gate is numerical: rank-normalised split $\widehat{R}$ at most `{python} num(BF['convergence']['gate']['rhat_max'], 2)`, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least `{python} count(BF['convergence']['gate']['ess_min'])` and at most `{python} words(BF['convergence']['gate']['divergences_max'])` divergent transitions [@vehtari2021]. These diagnostics check that the chains agree with each other, that they hold enough effectively independent draws and that the sampler explored the posterior without numerical failure. The analysis plan says that if the gate is unmet after one rerun the model reports no headline. As first coded, the bound on $\Phi$ was a wall of zero density inside the sampler, a region it could not enter, which tripped the divergence diagnostic in the first fit and in the registered rerun (@sec-b1-appendix gives the counts). By the letter of the plan the model therefore reports no headline. We report one because we judge the divergences to come from how we coded the bound, not from the posterior, and the plan lets a coding error be fixed in a commit that says so. Sampling without the wall and then discarding the draws outside the bound, which is rejection sampling, targets the same truncated posterior; it gives `{python} words(BW["divergences"]) if BW["divergences"] else "no"` divergent transitions, $\widehat{R}$ at most `{python} num(BW["rhat"], 4)` and effective sample sizes of at least `{python} count(math.floor(min(BW["ess_bulk"], BW["ess_tail"])))`. The wall-coded draws give the same median saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} bn(B1_GATE_WALL, 2)` against `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 2)`. A reader who holds to the letter of the gate should read the forecast as failing it.

For each of the `{python} count(BRB["draws_retained"])` retained draws we draw `{python} words(D.B1["paths_per_draw"] // 2)` paths of the inputs for the determination years `{python} B1_FWD_SPAN` and their mirror images (the same deviations with their signs reversed), `{python} count(D.B1_PATHS)` paths, and apply both rules to each in rule arithmetic. The cash saving on a path is its share of spending saved times the central run's basic and new State Pension spending under the triple lock, scaled by the path's triple-lock level against the central path's. That identity reproduces the gross saving of each of the `{python} words(len(D.V1_IDENTITY['single_path_runs']))` paths we ran through the microsimulation one at a time, the two OBR paths and three simulated paths (@sec-simpaths; for the OBR long-term path with its stored triple-lock rates, which the rules do not set), and the stratified averages of the earnings scenarios, to within `{python} bn(D.v1_identity_max_bn(), 5)`. The net saving applies the ratio of net to gross saving in those runs, `{python} num(D.V1_RHO["rho"], 3)` (@sec-b1).

Two sets of checks bear on the model, and @sec-b1-appendix reports both in full. Posterior predictive checks compare the record with records the fitted model generates [@gelman1996]. No registered statistic of the forecast-error record lies outside the central `{python} pct(D.B1_PPC_BAND, 0)` of records replicated from the posterior. We also refit the model under two hold-outs, which withhold from each refit the errors that a forecast of that date could not have used or that share its target years, and score its four-year paths exactly as the two registered models were scored. It meets every limit but the one on the floor bias: both hold-outs sit at the floor-bias limit, so the scores cannot show that the model would have passed the test the first two failed.

### The forecast of the saving {#sec-b1}

```{python}
B1_SAME = D.B1["pay_same_share"][str(FINAL)]

B1_C = D.B1["central_rule_arithmetic"][str(FINAL)]["gross_bn"]
B1_MIDG = {q: D.b1(MID, "gross_bn", q) for q in D.B1_QS}
B1_REAL = {q: D.b1_real(FINAL, q) for q in D.B1_QS}
B1_SHARE = {q: D.b1(FINAL, "share", q) for q in D.B1_QS}
assert B1G["p95"] > D.B1_RHO["max_stored_gross_bn"]  # the prose flags the net 95th percentile
assert B1G["p50"] < D.B1_RHO["max_stored_gross_bn"]
assert B1G["p50"] < lo_g < hi_g < B1G["p75"]  # section 5.3 says so
```

@tbl-b1 and @fig-b1-fan give the forecast of the saving, and @fig-b1-dist its distribution in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. Its probabilities are posterior predictive: shares of paths drawn from the fitted model and its priors. If the forecast errors of `{python} B1_FWD_SPAN` are as large as those of `{python} B1_ERR_SPAN`, the median gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is about `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 0)` (`{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 1)`), half of the paths lie between `{python} bn(B1G["p25"], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1G["p75"], 1)` , and `{python} range90(B1G["p5"], B1G["p95"], bn)`; with every input bounded at zero the `{python} V1_HI` percentile is `{python} bn(B1_CLIP["p95"], 1)`: the forecast's lower tail of inputs is heavier than the record's (@sec-b1-sure). `{python} cap1(B1_HALF)` of the paths, `{python} pct(100 * B1P[TEN], 1)`, save more than `{python} bn(TEN, 0)`, and `{python} pct(100 * B1P[FIVE], 1)` more than `{python} bn(FIVE, 0)`. The forecast rests on the record's errors: without `{python} V1_HOT`, the median is `{python} bn(B1_S7, 1)` and `{python} pct(100 * B1_S7_P10, 0)` of paths save more than `{python} bn(TEN, 0)`, and with shocks the size of past outturns' variation around their own mean, in place of forecast errors, the median is `{python} bn(B1_S12, 1)`. In `{python} fy(MID)` the median is `{python} bn(B1_MIDG["p50"], 1)`, and `{python} range90(B1_MIDG["p5"], B1_MIDG["p95"], bn)`.

On `{python} pct(100 * B1_SAME, 1)` of paths the two rules pay the same in every April to `{python} FINAL`. On the OBR central path itself the rule arithmetic saves `{python} bn(B1_C, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. The paths are centred on that path's inputs in every year, so the forecast's saving comes from the variation around them: a price- or floor-led April followed by earnings-led ones opens a gap that never closes (@sec-formal), so the spread widens with the horizon and the distribution is skewed to the right.

Once income tax and benefits respond, the median net saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is `{python} bn(B1N["p50"], 1)`, and `{python} range90(B1N["p5"], B1N["p95"], bn)`. The net figures apply the ratio of net to gross saving in our microsimulation runs, which misses a run's net saving by `{python} pct(D.B1_RHO["rho_loo_mean_abs_error_pct"], 1)` on average and `{python} pct(D.B1_RHO["rho_loo_max_abs_error_pct"], 1)` at most when that run is left out. The largest gross saving among those runs is `{python} bn(D.B1_RHO["max_stored_gross_bn"], 1)`, and `{python} pct(100 * B1_ABOVE, 1)` of paths save more than that in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, so the net `{python} V1_HI` percentile extrapolates the ratio.

The thresholds are in cash. A path on which the triple lock rises faster also has a larger pension to save on: across paths, the median triple-lock level in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is `{python} pct(100 * (B1_RATIO - 1), 1)` above the central path's. At the central path's levels, which removes that factor, the median saving is `{python} bn(B1_REAL["p50"], 1)` (`{python} V1_LO` to `{python} V1_HI` percentile `{python} zero_or(B1_REAL["p5"], bn)` to `{python} bn(B1_REAL["p95"], 1)`) and `{python} pct(100 * D.b1_real_prob(FINAL, TEN), 1)` of paths save more than `{python} bn(TEN, 0)`. As a share of basic and new State Pension spending under the triple lock the median saving is `{python} pct(100 * B1_SHARE["p50"], 2)`, and `{python} range90(100 * B1_SHARE["p5"], 100 * B1_SHARE["p95"], pct, 2)`.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-b1
#| tbl-cap: "The forecast of the reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock relative to the triple lock, UK: the median and the 25th to 75th and 5th to 95th percentiles of the posterior predictive paths, and the share of paths with any saving and with a saving, on each row's measure, above £5bn and £10bn. Gross and net in £ billion, cash; gross at the central path's levels without the path's triple-lock level against the central path's; share of basic and new State Pension spending under the triple lock, %. Net figures apply the runs' ratio of net to gross saving and extrapolate it above the largest run. Conditional on the model, its priors and forecast errors as large as the record's; the mean and the largest path are not reported, because the forecast's lower tail of inputs is heavier than the record's."
def _q(f, d=1):
    return [num(f("p50"), d), f"{num(f('p25'), d)} to {num(f('p75'), d)}", f"{num(f('p5'), d)} to {num(f('p95'), d)}"]
body = []
for y in (MID, FINAL):
    body.append([fy(y), "Gross (£bn)"] + _q(lambda q: D.b1(y, "gross_bn", q)) + [
        num(100 * D.b1_prob(y, 0), 1), num(100 * D.b1_prob(y, FIVE), 1), num(100 * D.b1_prob(y, TEN), 1)])
    body.append([fy(y), "Net (£bn)"] + _q(lambda q: D.b1(y, "net_bn", q)) + [
        "–", num(100 * D.b1_prob(y, FIVE, "net"), 1), num(100 * D.b1_prob(y, TEN, "net"), 1)])
    body.append([fy(y), "Gross at central levels (£bn)"] + _q(lambda q: D.b1_real(y, q)) + [
        "–", num(100 * D.b1_real_prob(y, FIVE), 1), num(100 * D.b1_real_prob(y, TEN), 1)])
    body.append([fy(y), "Share of spending (%)"] + _q(lambda q: 100 * D.b1(y, "share", q), 2) + ["–", "–", "–"])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Year", "Measure", "Median", "25th to 75th", "5th to 95th", "Any saving (%)",
                           "Above £5bn (%)", "Above £10bn (%)"], body, "llrrrrrr")))
```

### What the forecast rests on {#sec-b1-sure}

```{python}
B1_PR = D.b1_prior_range()
B1_ALL = D.b1_all_range()
B1_COND = D.B1["conditional_on_parameters"][str(FINAL)]
B1_A2 = D.b1_sup("a2")
LM = D.B1_SUP["i_level_misses_points"]
B1_D2, B1_D4 = D.b1_run("S9"), D.b1_sup("g")
B1_S4_95 = D.b1_run("S4", stat="p95")
assert B1_A2 > B1G["p50"] and B1_D4 < B1_D2 < B1G["p50"] and B1_D4 < B1_PR[0] <= B1_D2 <= B1_PR[1]
# Fat tails (S4) move the 95th percentile furthest among the prior runs (the prose says so).
_p95 = [D.b1_run(k, stat="p95") for k in D.B1_REG_PRIOR_RUNS] + [D.b1_sup(k, stat="p95") for k in D.B1_PRIOR_RUNS]
assert max(abs(v - B1G["p95"]) for v in _p95) == abs(B1_S4_95 - B1G["p95"])
```

The forecast is conditional on the model, its priors and the record, and five features of them move it or bear on how far it can be relied on. First, the record. Its forecast errors from `{python} V1_HOT` dominate it; @sec-b1 gives the median without them and at the outturns' scale. Changing one prior at a time, for the persistence, the tails, the correlation and the scales of shocks in both records, and removing or doubling the long-run shift, puts the median between `{python} bn(B1_PR[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1_PR[1], 1)`; quadrupling that shift puts it at `{python} bn(B1_D4, 1)` (below). Every sensitivity run, listed in @tbl-b1-sens, puts it between `{python} bn(B1_ALL[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(B1_ALL[1], 1)`. Among the prior changes, fatter tails move the `{python} V1_HI` percentile most, to `{python} bn(B1_S4_95, 1)`.

Second, the measure. The OBR forecasts calendar-year growth, while the rules use September CPI and May–July earnings, so the record's errors include how far the statutory inputs differ from calendar-year outturns. Fitting the model to calendar-basis errors lowers the median by `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[0], 1)`, and by `{python} bn(B1_BASIS[1], 1)` against a statutory fit on the same cells, so about that much of the median comes from that difference. Adding it back as a separately estimated term that does not persist from year to year gives `{python} bn(B1_A2, 1)`, above the headline.

Third, the lower tail. The model's shocks are symmetric, so September CPI falls below zero in `{python} pct(100 * B1_CPI_NEG, 1)` of forward path-years, against `{python} words(B1_CPI_NEG_HIST)` year in `{python} words(B1_HIST_YEARS)` since 1989. Setting every negative input to zero leaves the median at `{python} bn(B1_CLIP["p50"], 1)` and lowers the `{python} V1_HI` percentile (@sec-b1). The upper tail and the mean therefore rest on inputs less plausible than the record, so we report neither the mean nor the largest path saving. On the forward paths earnings growth is below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * B1_FWD_FLOOR['forward_2027_2038']['floor_share'], 0)` of path-years, against `{python} pct(100 * B1_FWD_FLOOR['history_2001_2025']['floor_share'], 0)` of years over 2001–2025, the event that the baseline model overstated when it failed its test (@sec-paths-method); the centre's own earnings growth, `{python} pct(100 * min(B1_CENTRE_E), 1)` to `{python} pct(100 * max(B1_CENTRE_E), 1)` a year, is lower than the record's. The test's windows, which cover the inputs of `{python} FY_YEARS[0]` to `{python} FY_YEARS[-1]`, realised `{python} pct(100 * REAL_FLOOR, 1)` (@sec-paths-method).

Fourth, the long run. No forecast in the record runs past five years, so years five to twelve rest on the fitted persistence and on priors for a long-run shift that no data here estimate. The record does show persistent level misses: the statutory earnings input fell short of the spring forecasts made from June 2010 to March 2016 by `{python} num(-LM["origins_2010_2016"]["h3"]["earnings"], 1)` points on average three years ahead and `{python} num(-LM["origins_2010_2016"]["h4"]["earnings"], 1)` four years ahead, and exceeded those made from March 2017 to March 2022 by `{python} num(LM["origins_2017_2022"]["h4"]["earnings"], 1)` four years ahead. A wider long-run shift lowers the median, to `{python} bn(B1_D2, 1)` with its standard deviations doubled and `{python} bn(B1_D4, 1)` with them quadrupled.

Fifth, the parameters and the design. The median saving conditional on a single posterior draw of the parameters has a standard deviation of `{python} bn(B1_COND["gross_median_bn"]["sd"], 1)` across draws, and the share of paths above `{python} bn(TEN, 0)` runs from `{python} pct(100 * B1_COND["p_gross_above_10"]["p5"], 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * B1_COND["p_gross_above_10"]["p95"], 0)` between the `{python} V1_LO` and `{python} V1_HI` percentiles of draws. The Monte Carlo error of the median is `{python} bn(D.b1_se(FINAL, "gross_p50"), 2)`. We set the priors after seeing the whole record, and the prior on the shock scale is centred near the official one-year errors that the likelihood then fits, so those errors inform the forecast twice. The data move the shock scales and the tails; the posteriors of the persistence, the pass-through and the correlation stay close to their priors (@tbl-b1-priors), so those priors carry through to the forecast. The priors alone, with no data, give a median saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` of `{python} bn(B1_PRIOR_PRED, 1)`, against `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 1)` with the data, a prior predictive check [@gabry2019]. We designed the model after two others failed their tests; it is the seventh model set against the same short record, and its checks are reported, not applied as a pass rule (@sec-b1-method).

### Robustness: four scenarios and stated volatility {#sec-budget}

@tbl-scenarios gives the reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock, relative to the triple lock, on four scenarios, and @fig-scenarios the gross saving in each year. Two are single microsimulation runs. One is the OBR central path. The other, which we call the OBR long-term path, is our construction: it keeps the central path's inputs but pays the triple lock at the OBR's long-term triple-lock rate from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM`, which phases in to earnings growth plus `{python} obr_premium` points, and applies the adjusted rule to the same inputs, so the premium goes to the triple lock only. The other two take `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths of prices and earnings, each run through the microsimulation under both rules, and move calendar-year earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points a year lower or higher from `{python} FROM` (@sec-paths-method). We attach no probability to any of them, and the four do not form a probability interval; they check the forecast of @sec-b1 against single paths and against the first model's paths. @sec-v1 gives the distribution conditional on stated volatility, and @sec-c4 the second model's distribution of the share saved, with no cash figure.

On the OBR long-term path the saving is `{python} bn(w_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} bn(w_n, 1)` once income tax and benefits respond (@sec-net). Earnings lead CPI and the floor in every April from `{python} earn_from`, so the adjusted Triple Lock returns to its earnings path and then follows it, and the whole of the triple lock's excess counts as saving ($G_t = y_t$). The premium is the OBR's average allowance for years in which CPI or the floor beat earnings, and no path of CPI and earnings pays it every year.

This scenario bounds the share of spending saved from above under the OBR's convention, and only under it: the saving if the OBR's premium is paid in full and the adjusted rule pays none. Since $G_t \le y_t$ on every path (@sec-formal), the expected gap under that convention cannot exceed the triple lock's cumulated excess on this path, from the floor-led Aprils and the premium together, `{python} points(WS["total"], 2)` log points; because $1 - e^{-G}$ is concave, Jensen's inequality gives the same for the share of spending, `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)`. The argument reads the OBR's premium, an arithmetic allowance of `{python} obr_premium` points a year, as the expected log excess $\mathrm{E}[y_t]$ from the April `{python} SWITCH - 1` anchor. In cash the bound need not hold, because the triple lock's spending base rises with its excess, and the two co-vary across paths.

The two earnings scenarios give `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` and `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. They are averages over paths from the model that failed the test, carry the same failed condition, and are reported because the registered rule keeps them as scenarios whatever the verdict, not because they are more reliable than the average it withdrew. They are not a range around an unshifted case. Both lie between the forecast's median and its `{python} ordinal(75)` percentile; they are means over a failed model's paths and the forecast reports a median, so the comparison shows only that the two are of the same order. The adjusted rule's average gap is `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["minus"] / SIM_Y["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["plus"] / SIM_Y["plus"], 0)` of the triple lock's average excess (a ratio of averages). @sec-scen-appendix gives the arithmetic of the OBR long-term path, the scenarios' shares of spending, the split of their gap between the mean and the variation of their inputs, and a reweighting to the realised frequency of floor years, which lowers their gap.

A further check gives the distribution of the saving if September CPI and May–July earnings growth vary around the OBR central path as they did over `{python} V1_SPAN`, with and without `{python} V1_HOT` (@sec-v1): a sensitivity conditional on stated volatility, on which no test bears. The forecast's median, `{python} bn(B1G["p50"], 1)`, lies between its two medians.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: "Reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock relative to the triple lock, £ billion, UK, cash terms; in the final year also as a share of basic and new State Pension spending under the triple lock and as the log gap G between the rules, log points. The OBR central and long-term paths are single microsimulation runs, on which G = −ln(1 − share). The earnings scenarios are stratified estimates over the same `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths, each run through the microsimulation, ± the 95% Monte Carlo error; their G is the average of G over the paths (rule arithmetic), slightly above −ln(1 − share) of the average share because the logarithm is convex. The last two rows reweight the scenarios' paths to the realised share of floor years (@sec-scen-appendix): a diagnostic, outside the registered rule, with the saving at each scenario's own spending base; the lower-earnings row also raises mean earnings. A scenario envelope, not a probability interval."
def _cell(v, e, d=1):
    return num(v, d) if e is None else f"{num(v, d)} ± {num(e, d)}"
NAMES = {"central": "OBR central path", "wedge": "OBR long-term path (triple lock at the OBR's long-term rate from April 2032)"}
body = []
for s in D.scenarios([MID, FINAL]):
    name = NAMES.get(s["key"], s["name"] + f", average of {N_DRAWS} paths")
    v = s["values"]
    sh, she = SHARE[s["key"]]
    g_cell = num(100 * GAP[s["key"]], 2) if s["key"] in ("central", "wedge") else \
        _cell(100 * SIM_G[s["key"]], 100 * SIM_GE[s["key"]], 2)
    body.append([name] + [c for y in (MID, FINAL) for c in (_cell(v[y][0], v[y][2]), _cell(v[y][1], v[y][3]))]
                + [_cell(sh, she, 2), g_cell])
for k, label in (("minus", f"Earnings {MINUS_SHIFT}, reweighted (diagnostic)"),
                 ("plus", f"Earnings +{SHIFT}, reweighted, mean earnings held (diagnostic)")):
    tr = TILT_ROWS[k]
    body.append([label, "–", "–", num(tr["share"] * BASE_SC[k], 1), "–", num(100 * tr["share"], 2),
                 num(100 * tr["G"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Scenario", f"{fy(MID)}: Gross", f"{fy(MID)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Gross",
                           f"{fy(FINAL)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Share of spending (%)", f"{fy(FINAL)}: G (log points)"],
                          body, "lrrrrrr")))
```

Gross saving in each fiscal year from the switch on the four scenarios, £ billion, cash; the shaded bands are ± the 95% Monte Carlo error on the earnings scenarios' averages."
F.scenario_years();

### The OBR central path {#sec-paths}

```{python}
crows = D.path_rows(central)
floor_years = [r["year"] for r in crows if r["tl_source"] == "floor"]
after = [r for r in crows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
first_earn = next(r for r in after if r["tl_source"] == "earnings")
differ = [r for r in crows if D.differs(r)]
p50, p90, rnd = D.path("monthly_p50"), D.path("monthly_p90"), D.path("random")
```

The OBR central path is one smooth path. The floor sets the triple lock in April `{python} listing(floor_years)`; from April `{python} first_earn["year"]` earnings lead every year (@fig-central). The two rules differ in `{python} words(len(differ))` year`{python} "" if len(differ) == 1 else "s"`, April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ])`: after those Aprils the adjusted Triple Lock rises only by the floor, or by what brings it back to its earnings path, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["tl_weekly"])` a year under the triple lock and `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["bp_weekly"])` under the adjusted rule, and the saving is `{python} bn(c_g, 1)` (`{python} bn(c_n, 1)` net). The OBR finds the same for its forecast period: "`{python} obr_medium`" [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.50, footnote 17].

Right: how far the adjusted rule's full new State Pension sits below the triple lock's, in per cent; a gap this small is close to the log gap G between the rules in log points."
